What a difference 3 years makes. I'm looking at a 3060 12GB for some entry level AI learning since they're cheap now at around $200 in mid 2024. I also put together my first system in probably close to 20 years after using laptops and older used enterprise equipment for non-gaming use.

author: @snakeplissken1754

text:
They are absolutely not artificially enhancing the shortage. If anything I wouldn't be surprised if Nvidea is rushing through development to make an extremely stripped down 30xx card that they can make as fast as possible.

Prices going up as supply dwindles is just basic economics. Every product works like that and it's sometimes a bit annoying that so many expect PC parts to somehow be exempt from that. Companies sell products for as much as people are willing to pay. That's just how capitalism works.
If Nvidea brings out a 800 dollar card and AMD a 600 dollar one and both are the same power people will go for the 600 one. But if neither cards are in stock people will pay what they are willing to pay since there is nothing cheaper to buy instead.


If anything though I do think profits for Nvidea and AMD are down because of all this. After all the prices are so high because there are far less cards being sold. Also with chips being used in so many products they themselves have to pay a massive premium for those as well since of course they are low in the picking order next to government projects and other industries like cars. GPU's are even considered below other PC parts like RAM and CPU which is why their shortage hasn't been anywhere near as bad.

text:
In a free market, there is no prioritisation of essential services unless the government steps in and forces the issue. Moreover, I've never seen bleeding edge CPUs so cheap and readily available so I'm disinclined to buy the silicon shortage - especially considering that silicon is mined in the least likely places in the world to impose lockdowns. This, also, casts some doubt on the crypto-mining story too. The wholesalers saw a captive market, thanks to CoVID, got greedy, cranked up the prices then, well, time will tell but my money's on them getting caught with stock they can't unload. Wouldn't be the first time, either.

So if, like me, you want a good card, keep the money you're wiling to spend on it; and wait for the tomfoolery to play out to its gloriously comedic Chapter Eleven conclusion. Probably be a nice, next-gen 32 gB DDR6 4080 Ti for a reasonable price, by then....
author: @Mercurio-Morat-Goes-Bughunting

text: Bleeding edge CPU's don't use up more silicon than cheap ones. The cost is in manufacturing and testing and silicon prices don't affect those.
author: @MrMarinus18

text: ​ @MrMarinus18  Ditto GPUs. The the only difference is that there is a perceived demand created for GPUs by CoVID lockdowns when, actually, there is a much wider range of issues with different solutions impacting gamers and, especially, people coming into gaming because of the lockdowns. The fact that shortages are not being experienced with all chips, only those used in graphics cards and, I've heard, engine controller boards for vehicles and heavy machinery; means that the supply issue has nothing to do with related raw material shortages. The fact that suppliers are misidentifying the issue means they're lying about it - probably because they're engaged in price gauging. It's not like things like this haven't happened before. We used to get regular "shortages" in things like memory and hard disks which you could set your watch by.
author: @Mercurio-Morat-Goes-Bughunting

text:
@Mercurio-Morat-Goes-Bughunting  There is a resource shortage, just not a desperate one. However it means that companies can't really ramp up production since there is very little spare silicon to go around. There is enough to keep the factories going but not really much more.

In comparison to CPU's GPU's use a lot more silicon.
The computer industry is indeed a volitile one because there are very strong trends, product age quickly and manufacturing costs are high. It's very easy to waste money by making the wrong product and lose millions by choosing just the wrong model so companies are very reluctant to make more than they need so there isn't usually a lot of reserve.
And this is companies being cautious cause having excess stock isn't bad. After all that means you can make massive money during shortages. The issue though is that hardware ages too quickly so by the time that excess production would be needed it's already obsolete.

Making the guess of just how much to produce is massively difficult because it takes time to impliment. You need to predict what's going to happen because reacting means by the time things are in order the situation has already changed.
And nobody can see the future so quite often they overestimate or underestimate.
However while guessing it perfectly is ideal being undersupplied is preferable to being oversupplied. If you're undersupplied you can still sell everything while if you're oversupplied you quite likely have to destroy your own inventory that you spend money to make.
author: @MrMarinus18

text:
​ @MrMarinus18  There is no silicon shortage. A shortage of seawater would be more likely. Silicon is reduced from silica melt using carbon. Silica is the most abundant material in the earth's crust and silica mines draw from the purest reserves of any primary industry. So much so that if you pull a 99.50% assay on a prospect, it's still not nearly enough to be competitive. If African production so much as twitched, you'd have mines popping up all over the world, almost overnight. 

The rest is outdated. Vendors routinely deal with unstable market demand via a backorder system (where orders are placed before stock is manufactured) or, further down the chain, a pre-order system (where orders are placed before stock is delivered). It's no big deal and it's quite uncomplicated.

It is a fact that the big supply chains, in IT, have engaged in practices with criminal ramifications (bait and switch, reselling returns, selling seconds as new, lying to consumers about their rights, etc.) - and still do to this day - which you will discover if you ever order a good sample of memory in the mail. So inventing fictional shortages is not out of character for the industry and, let's face it, pretty much every IT industry "shortage" in the past has later proven to be highly questionable at best.
author: @Mercurio-Morat-Goes-Bughunting

text:
@Mercurio-Morat-Goes-Bughunting  And why would they want to do such a thing?
Not sell inventory that they do have?

Pre-orders help somewhat mitigate it though cancelling puts a bit of a damper on that effect and it also doesn't help against overstock.

In your complaints you seem to mainly be referring to retailers. Nvidia and AMD design cards and Nvidia makes cards. They aren't the ones selling them.

Shortages in the past have been quite well documented. The IT industry for the reasons I already mentioned just is an inherently volatile industry with high risk/high reward and with very high starting investments which makes it slow to react to changes in the market. Hardware getting outdated so quickly also means it's pretty much impossible to make stockpiles to buffer against disruptions because by the time a disruption hits that stockpile is already obsolete.

But you were right that silicon isn't the issue. The issue is that GPU's are in very high demand with data miners, consoles and pc gamers. CPU's aren't in as high demand as people don't replace them as quickly and you don't have miners buying them in massive numbers. Also still when it comes to transistors GPU's use many times more.
Also Ryzen CPU's not having integrated graphics doesn't help since it means a GPU is mandatory rather than optional so that sucks up all the low end cards as well and those cards aren't being made anymore.
author: @MrMarinus18
@Mercurio-Morat-Goes-Bughunting

text:
@Mercurio-Morat-Goes-Bughunting  
I'm more confused as to how they would coordinate this. After all doing stuff like this leaves the door right open for someone to deliver reliable products and pretty much invalidate every other one instantly.

I don't understand why you are so skeptical in regards to crypto mining. Since they use multiple cards the numbers add up quick.

It's "limited availability" that doesn't mean it's impossible. But the availability being limited means it's hard to ramp up production to keep up with the increased demand both from gamers and from crypto miners. Crypto mining also has risen with Covid as many people can't go to work.

The shortages aren't just because of covid though. chip usage has increased massively in the last few years with cars, appliences, the universal ownership of both tablets and phones and more. Demand has increased massively but it's hard right now to increase supply so there is shortage.
A shortage means there is not enough. It doesn't have to mean there is less than there was before. if supply increases by 25% (which it has for GPU's) but demand increases by 100% there is still a shortage.

You are right in that panic buying is a thing but those things don't last long at all. A month or two at worst before the panic dies down again. It is just that so many industries are reliant on chips and it will take a long time for new factories to come online.
It's not so much that Covid reduced the availability of chips. it's more so that it prevented or at least slowed the increase in production when it was needed.
author: @MrMarinus18

text:
@Mercurio-Morat-Goes-Bughunting  I'm not arguing that they are morally upstanding or that dirty bussiness tactics aren't taking place. I'm arguing they just aren't powerful or organised enough to control things.
Also though again the big companies prefer a stable market where they can sell out a consistent flow. They don't like huge fluctuations that requires expensive shuffling of inventory with risk of damaging them and leads to plenty of cases of under- or oversupply.

Thing is though jacking up prices is useless if you aren't going to take advantage of them and this has been going on for over a full year and with prices consistently high. If they had the power to end it they already would have since the longer it goes on and the more GPU's are sold the more the prices will go down eventually. You need to strike when the iron is hot, you shouldn't let it cool down.

Internally with Nividea trying to maintain it's lead and AMD trying to snatch the GPU market from them like the snatched the CPU market from Intel both would love to strike right now. With prices high and demand also high and especially with AMD's compatibility boost with their zen 2 Ryzen CPU now would be perfect to flood the market. Nvidiea is still slightly technologically ahead of them but with demand so high that is almost completely irrelevant. People will buy a 6800 for 400 over a 3070 for 800 any day.
If anything I think AMD is incredibly frustrated with this whole situation. Since they were catching up to Nvidia nicely especially now that they have a strong enough market share to make increased performance with matching parts viable and they have enough market dominance to convince developers to make special optimization for AMD parts. However with this situation quantity is all that matters and Nvidia is bigger so they have the edge there.

That dumping of products is indeed quite a slimy bussiness tactic but it doesn't really support your argument. Just why it would be in their interest to not sell as many products as possible.
The things you're also talking about are much smaller things. Like products in the thousands, not millions. I'm very aware that dumping is a thing but those are mistakes leaving them with a few thousand parts that are worth far below their manufacturing price so they just dump them where they can sell them for as close to their production price as possible to minimize loss. That's not reducing their own profits in any way since they weren't able to sell those products anyway.
author: @MrMarinus18

text:
@Mercurio-Morat-Goes-Bughunting  The point is: Companies don't like slowing down their own production for whatever reason. They can shift priority but not prioritzing the GPU market when it's at an all-time high is just stupid. Especially with the competition going on with AMD encroaching on Nvidia and Nvidia being fearful of having it snatched away like what happened with Intel.

Dedicated mining cards indeed aren't very popular but not because crypto mining isn't big. The issue with them is that they are only good for crypto mining so have far less inherent value than GPU's. Crypto currency constantly changes and so it's easy to go bust in that industry. With GPU values so high the GPU's serve as colladeral in case of loss.
Also a lot of those dedicated mining cards really aren't that much better than standard GPU's. Not to mention being essentially GPU's with a few features removes means the chip shortage affects them too to so they aren't that much cheaper either.
I also don't understand why the prices of mining cards being high means mining isn't big. If anything it indicates the opposite but just mining cards aren't being made in large numbers since that industry is still so much younger and is also extremely volitile so dedicated factories making mining cards is a risky investment.
author: @MrMarinus18

text:
​ @MrMarinus18  I've spent enough time around factories to know that companies don't have any issue with slow-downs in production. They just retool and churn out something else.

The products I'm talking about (cameras, CCDs, 15" + 17" CRTs, hard disks) easily sold in the millions but the point was that the total absence of business ethics in the IT industry means anything goes. 

I've seen enough "shortages" in the past to know that, in the IT industry, "shortage" is doublespeak for "price fixing". And that's exactly what's happening now. 

Price fixing. 

If a guaranteed payday were involved (there isn't), I could have a dozen 3090 Ti cards on my doorstep by the day after tomorrow because there is no shortage, whatsoever. Just bad value for money at 300-400% of recommended retail. That's what price fixing looks like; especially when everyone is crying "shortage". 

I'd wager, a lot of retailers are going to get burned by this when the bubble bursts.
author: @Mercurio-Morat-Goes-Bughunting

text:
@Mercurio-Morat-Goes-Bughunting  You say you have experience but you haven't really provided any compelling arguments as how they would benefit from it.

You don't retool if you are selling things. You retool when the products aren't selling. Just when was there a significant oversupply that warranted they switch their factory tooling?

Factory retooling is expensive so they don't do that unless they feel they have to.

Also your first argument doesn't make sense. Of course they have an issue with that. They retool because products aren't selling and that's why productivity was slowed. Because otherwise they would be making products nobody wants.


You come across as more jaded than experienced.

text:
Performance wise, it'll do the job in most cases but it'll still tank in some cases. One that comes to mind is when I played BO: Cold War zombies and went from 120-160 fps at rounds 1-8 or so, to about 35-55 fps past round 15 (though that was with literally everything set to ultra). That smaller bus and somewhat lower clock speed has a pretty significant impact at times, it would seem. 

Also, mine is paired with a r5 3600 and 16gb ddr4 (300mhz), for anyone curious. Got a prebuilt coz that was in stock and not too too overpriced (though still overpriced imo). Thinking the ram might be giving me slight performance drop on the higher end, but I wouldn't think so much as to be a major factor in the frame rate drop.

Don't get me wrong, overall I'm quite happy with it but it didn't blow me away quite like I was hoping it would, going from a 1060 to the 3060. Regarding the price points for the cards themselves I agree completely with Jay. It's fucking laughable when a gpu price can range from ~$450 usd to ~$1250 usd. The DAG used for mineing limits what cards can mine, the dag needs increaseingly large vram reqs. use to be able to mine with 1-2-4 gb cards, but not anymore on alot of miners. and as time goes on the DAG requirements will grow, makeing the vram requirements go up for the card being used to  mine to be able to mine at all. I asked if there was a list you could be added to for video cards and they let me know that they had just got a few 3060 cards in. I decided to buy the Asus Strix 3060. When I tried to pay for it the salesman had a problem trying to sell it to me because, apparently the card had been sold to a bot. He was pissed, and I think the sales staff was fed up with the fact that bots were scooping up cards and not giving anyone else a chance. He was determined to get me the card because I was physically there and he offered it to me at the time. He cancelled a bot order so I could buy it. I had to wait for about a half hour, which I understand because the demand is so insane that there are constant orders for anything remotely decent. Eventually I was able to buy the card. It will be a pretty good upgrade for me. I super appreciate that the staff worked extra hard for me to get this card than rather give it to a miner. Much respect for my local Canada Computers store, at least the staff I dealt with.

text:
V-RAM isn't just used for the frame buffer, Jay.

V-RAM capacity is ACTUALLY important even on low end systems for game engines that have borderless maps or otherwise progressively load and unload assets as you roam around the game. You know, like almost every game does these days. It's only going to get worse with the next gen console architectures.

A perfect example is Cyberpunk 2077. The detail density in the city makes differences painfully clear. If you have more vram, it'll load better textures, more unique npcs, more detail, etc. etc. ... and if you only want more performance? Well, ever notice stutters while a game is pulling an asset in to vram? Yea, doesn't happen if it's already in vram.

So to say more vram is pure marketing (even just at the low end) is ignorant. Completely ignorant.

... It's also why nvidia is dumb as hell for releasing their cards with so little RAM on some models. Must be desperate to keep gaming separate from work cards by literally nerfing the gaming cards.

author: @Revadike

text:
It's probably even worse than that. In highly concurrent situations like people spamming buy, it's not terribly uncommon for one request to get serviced before one that arrived earlier if the dominoes are in a row.

So, depending on system arch, not only can someone who submitted first end up second+ just due to network delays, but even if they get in to the system, unless it's written very carefully, the system itself won't even necessarily be first come, first serve all the time.

text:
The shuffle system is fucking terrible. It's the laziest and cheapest way for NewEgg to seem like it's doing something to fight scalpers without actually doing anything. There are plenty of other measures they could take to combat scalpers that would actually be effective but they would cost NewEgg money to develop and implement. The shuffle system is essentially a four lines of code random number generator. The scalpers still have the edge by a mile. People, like a few replying here, fixate on the one in a million chance they got a card while overlooking the months they spent in the shuffle and the millions of other people that never got through the shuffle. It's the same phenomena that causes people to believe in all those charlatans pretending to be psychics. (To be clear ALL psychics are charlatans.) They focus on the one time the shit heel was right and forget the thousand times they were wrong. 

You are playing NewEgg and the scalpers game. So the scalpers have to enter the shuffle with all the other purchasers. So what? It doesn't mean the playing field has been leveled. If it had been leveled people would have stopped bitching about not being able to get a card months ago when NewEgg first started the shuffle nonsense. If I am a scalper all I do to beat the shuffle is have my bot create a few thousand - or more - fake accounts. When one or more of those accounts come up in the shuffle I buy all I'm allowed to buy on that account. It wouldn't even cost me time because I could just set my computer to do the work while I sleep. In the end I still get all the cards I want and you will pay me for them on Amazon or sleazebay because that's the only way you're getting one until about late 2022 and it's not inconceivable that the shortage could even stretch into 2023 before availability gets back to pre-pandemic levels.

text:
@JackoBanon1  why do people keep saying this? Why are crypto currency’s the future? 

Aside from it being a decentralized currency and a form of “electronic cash” if you will, it offers nothing more to consumers. 

I get that it’s “safer” than a centralized currency like the US dollar for example. But until they can figure out how to get transactions approved much much quicker, it will never be more that a backing for other currencies. Sure the transactions are more secure, but you’d be hard pressed to pass on the burden to consumers. 

I can swipe my visa, get approved, and be on my way in under 60 seconds. Can’t do that with crypto. And I think people are going to have an extremely tough time making crypto a mainstream currency, simply because SOMEONE will need to take a risk to get these transactions approved as quickly as credit cards. As of now in my opinion crypto is nothing more than an idea. An amazing idea for sure, but I’m still curious as to why everyone thinks this is “the future” 

This is all just opinion obviously

text:
VRAM matters on low end if you are developing on a game engine. 

Try building production quality lighting in UE4 with 6GB VRAM... Well good luck! 

Low end GPUs with high VRAM are really nice to have for budget game developers.

For those who are wondering, yeah a crappy card can still be used in developing a game. Game engines generally crash during builds if you don't have enough RAM or VRAM, but your processing power only affects the time each build will take. Which is workable, as long as it doesn't crash at the end of a 3 hour lighting build because of memory overflow for example...

You might as well buy an RTX 2070. I have a MAX Q 2070 8gb Card and it runs flawlessly (AND IT IS MAX Q) If you are wanting to buy an RTX 3060, just wait untill prices go down on the 3070's. For Gaming, 8gb GDDR6 is perfect. Only when you are using strenuous applications will the 12 gb be useful. But even so, at that point you are more likely to be bottlenecked by your ram, and not your Vram.

Although this is going off topic, don't have a bad image of Max Q laptops, and gaming laptops in general. It depends on the company, but also because it clocks a lower voltage, it enables the laptop to avoid increase heat(Which increases the Longevity of the system) 
For someone who games in bed, it is ideal. For anyone wanting to buy a new system, check out the Gigabyte Aero series. They are really great laptops for the price, primarily because there is no bad feature to them and you can upgrade to 64gb of ram, and trust me, although many people frown on 64 gb of ram for its excessiveness, it will avoid bottlenecking and enable you to have many applications open at the same time and at this point, I don't know how I could run a system without it XD

I do not see the hype or logic of upgrading, as still every card that gets released still relies on software to run the card. Maybe one day we'll see Graphic cards not being so reliant on software? Drivers is software and the amount of times in January/February having to keep upgrading drivers to run a game was getting stupid. One week I had the latest drivers installed, the next another one comes out in Windows. 

Linux drivers for gaming has come an awful long way, but you still have to fiddle around to get rid of screen tearing, switching off  Sync To V Blank and Allow Flipping. Then going into the Advanced part and switching on, by ticking a box the Force Full Composition Pipeline, which basically switches off screen tearing when gaming, so no need for V-Sync to be switched on any more. Then you have to sort out DPI (Dots Per Inch) by adding a line to your xorg.conf file after saving your NVIDIA settings. Option         "DPI" "96 x 96" otherwise after rebooting with Force Full Composition on, you'll end up with a blank screen, won't be able to login. If you restart after saving your settings without Force Full Composition on, your fonts are really small, hence why we need to do the above with Force Full Composition and the Dots Per Inch settings. Now you would think that after all this time, especially now as Linux is only a few numbers away with NVIDIA Drivers from Windows, that NVIDIA would include the Dots Per Inch in the Drivers? Windows is all there for you, but you have to have V-Sync on to get rid of screen tearing, or I do anyway in Windows. 461.72 Driver in Windows and in Linux 460.39, so we are not that far behind.

text:
One minor note about the 12GB VRAM; it's very niche, but livestreamers can put it to use. Running a rendering delay (to sync up input sources) GOBBLES VRAM, as the sources are stored uncompressed and full-frame pre-compositing in video memory (in OBS). The more VRAM you have, the longer delay you can use. Not much of a problem on a well-optimized system, but if you're using an old USB 2.0 video capture device with around 2 seconds of capture and transport latency in a real-time gameplay livestream setting, it would be invaluable. No more reacting 'ahead' of in-game events.
Of course the proper fix is to get a modern capture card (PCIe or USB 3.0) and not deal with a ridiculous delay in the first place, but if you're grabbing a 3060 you might not have that in the budget.
But! That VRAM can also be used for real-time compositing effects, looping delays, pixel shader buffer bashing, and other creative mutilations in a similar vein that love to just chew through a big stack of memory.

text:
"12GB is a marketing gimmick"

Yes and no. The issue is that they had a choice between 6GB and 12GB, and the card likely benefits from having more than 6GB. The GPUs themselves are designed to address a certain number of VRAM channels, and they need 32 bit of bus per channel. 192 / 32 = 6. With 1GB per channel (like on the 3060Ti, 3070, & 3080) that comes to 6GB. With 2GB per channel (like on the 3090) that comes to 12GB. Those are their only options given the silicon that they have.

text:
I think the "marketing circlejerk" thing may be wrong from what I've heard. 192-bit being the same as 3x 64-bit (where you can have 64-bit addressing to non-ECC memory ranks) would mean you could have: 512MBx3 = 1.5GB / 1GBx3 = 3GB / 2GBx3 = 6GB / 4GBx3 = 12GB -- but not 8GB or 16GB. It's the balance point, where 6GB wouldn't be enough, but 12GB would be a little overkill. Not being able to have access to 256-bit memory bandwidth (due to having to bin GPUs, some of which may not be usable with a 256-bit bus) would mean they would have to make this compromise.

EDIT: You do make a good point about the inability to use the extra memory due to people running it at a lower resolution with some of the newest games. Since people aren't making use of the extra memory size (smaller texture size), then it may not be worth them having more than 6GB VRAM on the cards. Then again, on some older games there is the possibility to use much more than 6GB VRAM and benefit from it while running 3840x2160. It's capable of running games at that resolution, and people are going to use that resolution. The 3060 would work well under those circumstances where people are running "4K", albeit with other graphics settings at a lower setting for the higher fps.

I just watched your video.  1st I feel your pain on the COVID.  Get better soon.

Now the reason I'm here. It is funny how you mentioned the waiting on line at Microcenter.  I pulled in to the parking lot of the 1 in New Jersey at around 9am for about 2 minutes.   I noticed about 6 cars parked, idling and about 4 chairs where there should have been people, if this were a proper line queuing for  a high demand item, right by the store entrance. There were opened and unopened chairs in spots where there should have been human beings. Then 2 minutes later I noticed some people rushing out of their cars to the so called, empty line and starting some sort of commotion.   I figured, Oh, wow, the  store must be opening up early since people all of a sudden started walking abnormally fast towards the chairs.   There was even one person  rushing out of her vehicle, in what resembled a bathroom & pajamas with slippers, walking very fast towards the chairs.  But as I walked towards the line I noticed it was people arguing about spots that should have been filled by people instead of empty chairs or folded chairs holding spots. Ibhung around to confirm what I was witnessing.  This rant went on for about 10 minutes as I just watched and tried to decide whether or not it was worth my time getting on the line and possibly watching something like this escalate to something bad. text:
This is not about marketing, the 12GB is about an engineering choice.

With only 8GB the Card would be severly bandwith starved, only having a 128bit bus, which is not enough for the 28SMs / 3584 shaders.  
6GB on the other hand fits well with a 192bit bus, but is the same as the  6 year old 1060 6G and the 2060 6G, which are  limiting already todays games at 1080p. So clearly 6Gb isn't enough in 2021. Nvidia could have pulled a GTX970 again with 8Gb total and only 6gb being fast and the other 2GB very slow, but remember the last time this ended up with them getting sued.

The card not being able to utilize its 12GB at all is clearly wrong.  there are scaling Tests which puts the 3060 ahead in several games vs the 3060ti  already at 1080p.  Especially when raytracing is enabled, the 8gb on the Ti und 3070 are limiting performance in watchdogs legion and minecraft RTX so much that the vanilla 3060 is up to 50% faster. https://www.pcgameshardware.de/Geforce-RTX-3060-Grafikkarte-277122/Specials/RTX-3060-Was-bringen-12-GByte-1367634/

This is the Card with RTX for the masses, the one many will be using for the next 5 or 6 years like the 1060 now. This will not be upgraded as frequently as a highend card like the 3080.  I think in this case 12gb make a lot of sense.

Also you are not very well informed about AMDs plans. It has been clear since almost a year that the 6700 Series will come with 12GB of VRAM, having the same 192bit Interface width as the 3060.

I'll save my money, and try my best to squeeze the last juice out of my trusty old Asus GTX 970 card (which I bought for about $100 lower back then), until the market kind of balances out again, and stock doesn't become a problem.

text:
Yes, it sucks that we are not able to buy these new parts, and that it's being handled so poorly is also annoying, but what I'm also a little tired of is effectively blaming Nvidia and the IBPs and what not for the frankly unprecedented state of our society world wide, and in the same breath also blaming them for our clearly broken and deeply flawed global economy. 
Could they have handled the pricing better? Yes, obviously. Could they have built a product which makes more sense? It would seem that way. The amount of memory is a hella weird choice for damn sure.
But perhaps there was a missed opportunity here for a fresh take on, and bear with me and take a deep breath before I say: talk about how getting upset and cranky and frustrated at a time like this does nobody any good? and it might perhaps be more constructive to try and learn to accept the situation and remember that this too will pass. As is, this video comes off a little too much like a self-entitlement support group talk than a professional review of a product.
It's pointless to blame Nvidia or board partners for being a company with a goal to generate revenue and profit. Is it annoying? Fuck yes, but no matter the tantrums you pull, you won't change a damn thing about it. It is equally pointless to out our frustrations about the state of our collective existence on these companies, or on anyone else for that matter. It is not their fault.
Yes times are hard, and patience is at a premium, but perhaps we should realise that we too are making decisions under unprecedented circumstances, within most if not all of our lifetimes at least, and that perhaps we too are not making the smartest choices in how we are reacting to this situation, and maybe that is an opportunity for some self reflection we might benefit from.
Thank you for the video, and Im glad you're on the mend Jay. Take care and look forward to what you'll work on next!

The thing that confuses me is why so many seem to have the idea that PC parts should for some reason be exempt from how the economy works. I mean what good is "it should cost this" if nowhere is the price anything like that? PC parts are just like any other product; it's worth what the consumer thinks it's worth and that is by supply and demand. If they can get a cheaper one that works just as well then they won't buy it. However that's not the case. Rather the 2060 is older or not is totally irrelevant, it's not cheaper and that's all that matters.
Once AMD and Nividia get their stocks back up prices will drop. Again that's just how economy works.

Also the the whole 12GB being a marketing gimmick. I'm not so sure cause it's either 6GB or 12GB cause of the way it's designed.
Having a faster card with less RAM for gamers and a slower card with more RAM for content creators makes sense. That way they are not competing with themselves.

If you don't want to buy inflated prices, don't buy products when they are scarce.

text:
@NebulonRanger  Wait until you're 60 or older. When your system is overwhelmed by medical tourism, your hospitals/staff aren't funded properly and there's just too many patients for not enough doctors, the doctors have to prioritize and the old are literally left to die. Also if treatment is too expensive (like aids), they won't allow you to pay more, even if you want to, and will, de facto, have to die.
The US might not be the best system in the world, but honestly, WITHOUT INSURANCE (in all caps because insurance causes the exact same issues: you lose your right to chose your treatment), USA is hands down the best system I've seen.
First because you can actually get the treatment that's super expensive and survive, versus not having the treatment. I'd rather be poor than dead. Second because of the high cost, it prevents abuse of the health system (people going to the hospital for a mild cold and clogging up the hospital).

I've worked a lot in many hospitals in the US and have seen with medicare/medicaid/insurance and without. I've seen France too where insurance through the state is mandatory (much like Canada).

Now from what I've seen in Canada (I help americans and french canadians communicate), the system is not overwhelmed YET. But with your policies on immigration, and low skills workers coming with low salaries (when they have a salary at all), it's just a matter of time before you become just like France and have to wait 8 hours before seing a doctor in the hospital because the whole world decided to get treated for free at your hospital.

There are many many things that should be said, like the myth that insurance and government intervention lowers medical costs when it's the exact opposite. With insurance, I would pay $800 for a trip at the ER (mandatory exams + copay of $250).

Without insurance, the same trup costs me $125 (the doctor can skip exams that are unecessary, and since the insurance doesn't fix the prices, the hospital is willing to lower the princes, it's called a sliding scale. So in the end insurance drives prices up, not down. Insurances, just like casinos, never lose money. You, the client, will always be the loser, no matter what lies they feed you. Insurances aren't a charity, they're here to make money. Your health doesn't matter to them or your politicians.

text:
I paid more than $100 over MSRP for the 'Sapphire RX580 Nitro+ SE' I bought during the height of the bitcoin mining boom a few years back. (how many names can you give a single video card?). No way in hell am I shelling out anything for a card in the current market. Some of these GPUs cost more than the 19 year old near perfect condition four wheel drive truck I bought for my wife last year, and the truck will be useful for much longer than the GPU. 

Forget that the cards were overpriced to begin with. There's no excuse for the cards' MSRP to be as high as they are in the first place. No. Don't give me that shit about how it's a supercomputer that has more power than the CPU of the machine you're installing it in. 

Yeah, I know it's true, but show me how to leverage that for myself if I'm not rendering video (almost exclusively only available to NVIDIA cards) or mining some dodgy digital currency. 

You can't because it doesn't exist. Windows, Mac, Linux, none of them offload any CPU computing loads to the GPU under normal operations. Unused video RAM isn't made available for holding a bigger spreadsheet or holding more browser tabs. 

If you can't load an operating system on it, it's not a 'supercomputer', it's a fucking peripheral. And there's no valid reason it should cost as much or more than the entire rest of the computer.

text:
The shuffle is also populated by bots - it 'just' takes more bot entries to skew the drawing odds and screw over everyone else who plays by the book and just enters once, plus it puts more of an incentive towards also entering for package deals where you only really want one of the components in the package, simply because it's a legitimate way to slightly increase your odds of winning either the single component you want, or the wanted component along with other stuff you can sell off if you're drawn.

It does however completely negate transparency when they don't publicly show how many entries exist for the products; if you KNOW you're #637 in line waiting for a card, and they get 10-15 cards each month, you can derive that it's probably not worth the wait - if you don't even know how many entries are in a shuffle, you have no way of knowing even roughly your odds at being drawn, you could be at a 50% chance(lol phat chance) or a 0.0000000000000001% chance.

JAY the dies are completely different, all 102 dies are the same within an architecture, same with 104 or 106 & onward each code is a different die. You cant just cut a 102 die in half and get say 2 106 dies. There are memory controllers, pcie and display out along the edges and the cores in the middle.
Although you can have a 104 die "limited/cut down" to 106 specs into a 106 card but the die would be 104 sized and should carry the "XX104" prefix. 
example - EVGA 2060 KO TU104-150 when 2060 was TU106-200

text:
The reason it has 12Gb VRAM is because the 192bit bus can't address 8Gb at full speed. Nvidia had a choice between 6Gb and 12Gb VRAM. 6Gb isn't enough. That's fact.

8Gb VRAM would have been more expensive because it would require a larger 256bit bus. That means a larger die, lower yields, more traces on the PCB, more transistors. It would push the price up to the 3060Ti

The 3060 could have had 8Gb with a 192bit bus but the last 2Gb would have had to share it's bus with another module which would have reduced the bandwidth of anything over 6Gb by 50%. Just like they did with the gtx 970 where the last 0.5Gb had shared bandwidth.

So 12Gb VRAM is the best solution and not just a marketing circle jerk.

Why don't any of the tech channels understand bus speed addressing?

text: jay just a heads up, more v-ram is really handy for being able to add more textures at higher resolutions to a game, these textures also include multiple version's of the same texture that are color coded differently to create the bump maps, normal maps, specular maps etc... each one of these "maps" is a separate texture that is loaded to the gpu's vram so the game engine has the information needed so it knows how to render each texture correctly when they interact with dynamic lights, in the games environment. the problem is with not having enough vram is you are now limited to the amount of textures you can have in the area or field of view and also the resolution of those textures. more v-ram is better with out a doubt and its the only way you going to get next gen visuals without a big performance hit to fps compared to rtx or a game that uses heavy workloads of shaders in the game. hd textures are the cheapest way to decorate a game's environment and make it look good and look next gen. think of a games environment as a 3d photo if you had the ability to 3d scan a small city block and you had the v-ram capability of holding terabytes of storage. you could use a 1 single mega texture to cover the whole area and have the visuals of 16k resolution, things will start to look very realistic very quick and the performance hit will not really be noticeable as once the texture is loaded the game only has to display the image as its just a picture applied to a 3d object.

text:
I actually like the Newegg shuffle.. because it's the ONLY chance I even have to get one of the new products.   After having alerts running for over a month before giving up, I wish more e-tailers followed suite.

And I also disagree with all the reviewers discrediting the 12GB VRAM on the cards.  Sure, the card isn't meant for 4k, but it's not like it can't do it (especially with DLSS).  And regardless, having the VRAM buffer lets you use high quality settings in games (notably 4K texture packs which chew through VRAM), where your resolution *does not matter*.  It also provides benefits outside of gaming as well.  Really, no card should be coming out with less than 10GB VRAM at this point in time; it significantly lowers its value and future proofing capability.  AMD is doing it right, and forcing NVIDIA to try to match them; and the 3060 vs the 3060 Ti shows this in spades.  Makes NV look like the doofus instead for once.

text:
Sorry, but as happens sometimes, Jay is just wrong. 12GB might not be "necessary", but it is far from "nothing but a PR move". 

The fact is, no matter how slow the bus, it's still far faster than fetching stuff you've had to store in system RAM because you ran out of VRAM. The usefulness will certainly vary, and you can argue you could just lower textures etc. But straight up running out of VRAM is far more detrimental than just losing FPS on account of not keeping up with processing. 

12GB on this card makes it last longer, end of story. You can keep dropping resolution or post processing effects etc to make up for the processing power. But if you ever simply don't have enough VRAM to play with anymore, there's nothing you can do.

If you buy a new card every year, very unlikely this will ever affect you. But if you hold on to cards for longer then this gives it a longer life, so long as you can deal with less and less frames/less and less fanciness. 

Lastly, as far as I can tell, GDDR6 is fabbed on 10nm, so doesn't affect the 7/8nm nodes that nVidia and AMD fabricate their stuff on. Intel does fab on 10nm, but at least for now they have their own fabs, so this isn't the same pool of silicon.

EDIT: I'd just like to add that I do think AMDs 16GB of VRAM is a much better target for "purely PR". That amount of needed VRAM is so far off in the future that it is unnecessary. I think they would have been much better off with 12GB also. That said, GDDR6 is so cheap, I don't really mind. But they are a much better target than this 12GB for playing PR games.

So +10% of price, for around 20% better performance with this 3060.
Same tier performance of 2060 Super, same tier of price.
But, in the real world with scalped price, the cost will be higher even in comparison with 2070 Super, that is defenetely faster.
Further, while 3060 Ti have slightly better performance than 2080 Super (399 vs 699 MSRP), 3060 have slighlty better performance of the 2060 Super (329 vs 399), this after adopting new node and architecture.
Even the efficiency is nearly the same (170 vs 175 Watt of TDP).
Other datas: 3060 Ti, with 25% lower price than the 3070, have only 10% less the performance. 
3060 with 21% lower price than 3060 Ti, have 25% to 30% less the performance, so the performance/cost ratio is worse. If we consider that GA106 is way smaller than GA104, and that GA106-300 used for 3060 is a cut-down of the full chip (32 vs 28 SMs), they charging premium price on a lower-end product, that is simply ridicolous, a really shame.
Some quotes:

"Last gen flagship performance, for last gen mid range pricing, not last gen 5700 performance for f*ucking 5700 XT pricing two years later, nobody ask for this." - Moore's Law is Dead

"Nvidia at this point realized that their products do not have to be exciting. They just have to exist." - Gamer Nexus

Yep at $329 this would have been a great card for sure. I also seen a quite a few complaining oh it sucks it is not as fast as a 2070 Super. I laugh every time I seen a deranged comment like that because this 3060 card was not made to beat a 2070 Super it was made to replace a 2060 card and be faster than a 2060.

It does that asy enough and matches a 2070 card I would say mission completed. As for the pricing I was rather pissed off to see $550-$650 prices listed about a week before the 3060 was even released by Nvidia. So it was a given that retailers and card makers were already planning to scalp the consumers by over charging the customers.

What we need put into place by government is some sort of law that forces retailers & product makers charge what is listed on the spread sheets by the parent product maker and if they go over by a certain amount they face very very very hefty fines enough so that it would have to make the rethink fricking over the customer base. I know this fricks with free market pricing and all of that crap but I have one thing to say about this free market pricing thing and that is fuck them they had their chances over and over again to treat their customers with repsect and they fricked it up way to many times and we need to have drastic measure put into place to put these companies back in their place and in line.

I noticed the trend of over pricing and then the excuses they use to justify them over pricing is getting more lame each year. Most people complain about it online and shake their fists at these companies and yell and scream at them over the internet and then they still go out and buy the over priced products.

You want to stop them form using these tactics on their customers it is really simple stop buying their products but we all know that is never going to happen so that is why I said the governments need to get involved and use their god powers to put these companies on notice cut them all down a few pegs or notches. Normally I would be the last one to say hey we need the gov to stick their noses into everyone's business but I truely do not see anything else working. 

If we continue to let these companies do this in a few years a top end gaming card will be like 15K USD and an entry level what should be a $125 card will be $750-$850 USD. Some will say of the tin foil hat guy is speaking crap but mark my words if we let them continue down this path this is where the prices are heading in the future.

I am fine with my own card I got a Vega 64 and I got it for $369 CAD on a flash sale a ways back when they were still selling for over $650 CAD before the 5700 & 5700XT came out. I am good to be able to wait it out until hopefully these retailers and card venders get some common sense and of coarse stock if not I will just drop PC gaming at some point when my card no longer is able to run the current games at full FPS and just get a console and be happy. I hear Xbox game pass is a pretty great deal any ways but I hate console gaming or at least I did in the past when they all were stuck at 30 FPS but now with 60 FPS and VRR they have become a decent option and a lot cheaper as well than a full gaming rig.

One can only pray things will improve in the summer. 5800x, 6800xt, ASRock mobo, 32 Gb ram. That's the spec I have in my head.

text: The only options available to a 192-bit design are 6GB VRAM or 12GB VRAM. For $329, in 2021, consumers would simply see a 6GB card as insulting. The 1060 released 4.5 years ago for $249 with 6GB. The RTX 2060 released 2 years ago for $299 with 6GB. And the 2060 Super, which this should really be replacing, has 8GB, and much more memory bandwidth. It's true that 8GB is enough for the vast majority of gaming workloads, and 6GB isn't too bad. But AMD didn't go with 16GB VRAM just for marketing purposes. It's partially just a forward thinking move (finewine), and partially because they knew they couldn't put 6GB on their down market cards. But another chunk of the equation is that they're hoping to gain mindshare and marketshare in GPU-compute. They don't segment or lock down their gaming vs. workstation cards nearly as much as NVidia does. The only way people with certain workloads (3D modeling, 4K/8K encoding, deep learning) can get a card that might meet their needs without spending ~$2k+ on a 3090 or Quadro is to go AMD. Or at least that was the plan before the crypto necromancers got busy again.

text: You are wrong about the shuffle being a bad idea.  It isn't ideal, but it is better than a simple queue for a lot of reasons (I am sitting in the not-moving EVGA queue as I sit here).  First, it refreshes.  That means it won't fill with a million people/bots and when/if they get picked, are not going to buy, causing millions of dead entries.  Second, it doesn't require you to slam a web site at some arbitrary instant -- with 100000 others -- to try to have a chance.  Like trying to get a good position on a Southwest Airlines flight.  It really is one of the better ideas.  But I hate that it is so opaque.  We don't know how many units are available, how many people we are up against (generally, what our chances are), and they do not ever announce it in advance, despite that it would be easy to do so.  Give this some more thought, and by all means say how you think it should be done.

text:
At this point, I feel like the only way to get a new card is to suck it up and stand in line :/ 
Best buy literally wouldn't even update for me until 18min AFTER and that's when I found them to be out of stock. Ridiculous!

I'm coming from a 765 GTX M so ANYTHING would have been better and yes I did react out of desperation but before my standing in line experience at MicroCentre, I didn't know if I was going to be able to get a card at all.

I went to MicroCentre around 1830 and a line started around 2300. Around 0700, I guess the stockers showed up and informed us there were cards instock (150 of them!) and since I was 7th in line, I knew I would get one AND have a choice of which SKU. I shamelessly chose the Gaming X at 512usd.
My point is that, if you REALLY want a card, going to a store might be the only way to secure one. Also, super important above all, make sure you're no more than 20th in line. Any position after 20 in line and you risk not getting anything on launch day if they don't have many cards; just my 2cents.

I understand not everyone has the luxury of doing the 1.5 day line wait but if you have someone willing to do so or if you know a line waiting service (don't know what they're officially called, I know there are services where you can pay someone to do the line wait for you) I'd say those would be your best options.

As for the Ti versions of the '70 and '80, you bet your ass I'll make it priority to be first in line on those release days because lay Jay explained, I can imagine that those models would be in very short supply on launch day (just my hypothesis).
...still waiting for Nvidia to launch the new 30 series gpu I keep hearing about.

text:
The fact that product reviewers like JTC, LTT, GN and Hardware Unavailable are now barely receiving the products to review pretty much illustrates the problem. They've all received the same base model, bottom of the stack, EVGA 3060 XC Black, the cheapest card available, from Nvidia directly, not the AIBs, because the AIBs know that right now they don't need any help to sell the products. Anything available will sell instantly, regardless of where it lies in the product stack and how it compares to its peers and at a massively inflated price to boot.

I suspect the only reason Nvidia has sent these bottom rung cards out to reviewers is to essentially keep the channel open, as it were. They're at least considering the future somewhat, and want to maintain the minimum level of back-and-forth between themselves and the PC Enthusiast community.

Obviously recovering from Covid-19 takes priority, but if you're feeling run-down over the whole GPU situation, what about changing your focus towards products that are available? I particularly enjoyed your review of the Azza Overdrive, your case reviews are much easier to 'digest' than GN for example. You mentioned the possibility of doing a build in that in the video. The XOC videos with the Kingpin 3090s are also entertaining.

Maybe do a video about Power Supplies? It's something that's often overlooked and not properly understood by a lot of people. Break down features like undervolt protection and how that can affect your system if you don't have it. I know they're pretty obvious but there's the pros and cons of modular and non-modular, how modular is typically a little more expensive but neater and allows for things like cable-mod cables, non-modular can be easier for the inexperienced but might not have all the PCI-E power cables you need if you've got, say, a triple 8 pin GPU. The difference between ATX, SFX and SFX-L. The length can be a factor in some cases, like my MSI Gungnir 100; if the PSU is longer than 180mm you're going to have to remove the 3.5" drive bay, thereby limiting your storage options.

text:
Oh it gets worse. Cars weren't selling last year so the manufacturers prioritized electronics, including consumer electronics believe it or not.

But when the component orders have to be placed ahead of time, often in weeks. Then shipped over on a massive diesel cargo ship. The problem cascades into months.

It doesn't help that Toyota popularized JIT (just in time) manufacturing techniques a while back. Everyone stopped maintaining inventory in favor of cost and "efficiency". Everything computerized... orders placed sometimes months ago timed to arrive in a holding area just before use.

A pandemic hit, and nobody was left holding enough inventory to push through even PART of it.

JIT manufacturing was great for profit margins. It was nice for companies that didn't want to be left holding large, unsold inventories, but as we can all clearly see, it isn't resilient to even moderate supply chain disruption.

text: You say that such a big ram size is stupid becuase the framebuffer (i.e. resolution) won't ever realistically be that big on such a low performance card, which is true specifically about the framebuffer size, but you're ignoring the point that  what that memory is really intended for is working space for RTX and DLSS and before-render content (models, maps etc). you're also ignoring that graphic content is getting bigger and bigger with every new AAA game that comes out. GPU performance can be MUCH faster when it is caching content locally rather than having to repeatedly grab it on-demand across the (relatively slow) PCIe bus because it doesn't have enough ram to store it locally.

They know they cant manufacture enough to meet demand, but they know if they charge for double, people will still buy it, and the governing body that should regulate price gauging aint doing shit.

text:
Actually I believe 3060 chip (GA106) is not a cut down/lower bin chip from anything that Nvidia have released so far. 3090 and 3080 share the same chip (GA102), 3070 and 3060 ti share the same chip (GA104). So they produced this chip specifically to target the mid low to low end market (although even at MSRP, $330 is hardly a mid low pricing for most people). 3050 probably will use this same chip, but right now, only 3060 is using GA106. So saying that Nvidia making this because of left over or something is probably not correct. For people wondering why they have these different chips instead of using 1 chip and bin it aggressively, the problem is that the supply is going to be too unreliable. If 30% good enough for 3090, 50% good enough for 3080, then what? you're left with 20% to make 3070, 3060 ti and 3060. That is simply not enough. You can balance it by potentially selling chip that perform better to be use on the lower tier product, but that is basically throwing away money (it has been done before tho, but normally they want to avoid this). Also by using 1 chip (so basically using the biggest chip) then it will be harder to make it cheap, also will be harder to produce it in quantity. The chip size (die size) for GA102 is 628 mm², GA104 392 mm², GA106 276 mm². By producing several chips tailored to different tier they can make more GPUs and price it accordingly.
As for shuffle, depending on how it's done, it is actually a good thing. It is actually a lot more fair using the shuffle vs first come first serve. First come first serve is not something you want to do for items that is going to be limited in quantity. As long as the store can make sure that there is not going to be a duplicate buyer (in Japan, they do this by using your ID), then everyone can take their time to apply for the product and wait for the result. This way they can avoid large scale scalpers and stop people from being glued to the store/keep pressing F5. Yes, it is definitely a hassle, especially for people that actually need a new GPU right now, but unless you have some unicorn system that can tell this person deserve more than the other person, having a shuffle/lottery is not something you should dismiss unless you actually have a better solution that can be more fair to everyone.

text: Just want to point out, these cards are not low performing versions of previous dies, just cut down because they did not make the cut for the higher tier.  The 3060 is the only GA106 based card nvidia is making currently, the 3060ti actually is a cut down GA104, and 3080 is a cut down GA102.  Nvidia benefits because the smaller dies generally have a significantly better yield so they could theoretically make a lot more cards with the same amount of silicon, though we probably will see some 3050ti or something like that as a cut down GA106 to make money on the few chips that have some issues.  (This is also likely true for AMD, the upcoming whatever will be based on the Navi 22 die, not the much larger Navi 21 that the 6800, 6800XT, and 6900XT are all on)  Overall agree with the main thrust of the video though. text: Correct me if I am wrong, but from my understanding, the 3060 has 12GB of VRAM because of it's 192 bit memory bus, unlike it's Ti counterpart with has the 256 bit memory bus. I once read a few years ago that each 32 bits of memory bus connects to one package of GDDR, which is manufactured in amounts of power at either 1GB or 2GB. Although you could technically use 8 GB VRAM with the 3060, it would lead to non-uniform performance. With a 192 bit bus, the ideal configurations are either 6GB or 12GB of VRAM. If you divide 192 by 32, you get 6. If you multiply 6 by the GDDR packages of 1GB or 2GB, you get 6GB or 12GB of VRAM. So I guess where I am going with this is, is it purely a marketing strategy, or was it partly due the GA106 not likely being able to take advantage of the 256bit bus?

text:
It isn't "capitalism" when it isn't a free market, and atm we do not by any means whatsoever have a free market, re the vast plethora of govt restrictions in the supply chain, delays to shipment procedures, border control policies, staggering levels of govt printed/borrowed money which is inflating the market, etc. So place the blame where it truly lies: pandemics do not cause shortages, govt responses to them do.

As for "scalpers", again that's just an excuse to dodge where the core responsibility lies in the demand cycle, namely, with the buyer. Market situations such as this are demand-driven; it's not scalping to raise prices to control demand. If you stop retailers from raising prices as they should be able to (free market) then by definition that facilities a margin gap which will be exploited, and you don't get to decide what someone does with a product they buy. Price fixing creates black markets and price distortion, it always has, whether it's done via govt edict or consumer/media pressure. In a demand-dominated market, you have to choose between higher standard pricing or black markets, so stop complaining about govt policies and consumer behaviour which block the former and encourage the latter at the same time.

https://libertarianinstitute.org/articles/why-price-gouging-actually-helps-during-a-crisis/

This stuff is 101, Jayz. Atm the only channel which explains it properly is Bryan of Tech Yes City. Paul of NAAF touches on it too sometimes, but not so deeply as Bryan, though Tom of MLID has explained many times how all the companies are exploiting what's going on for their own gain. As long as consumers are willing to pay the prices though, and as long as they have spare cash to burn for all sorts of reasons (I recall people referring to stimulus cheques as, "2080 Ti tickets"), then this cycle will not end. Those who complain about price increases but at the same time accept govt handouts which they spend on non-essential tech products are being very hypocritical, their actions are adding to the inflationary pressures. I've seen many PC parts prices in the last 3 months increase by the equivalent of as much as 500% p/a.

Don't even get me started on crypo... :\

https://static.coindesk.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/03/Bitriver-farm-710x458.jpg
https://assets.bwbx.io/images/users/iqjWHBFdfxIU/ih97FyDk72Xc/v0/1800x-1.jpg
https://www.cryptocurrency365.com/news/wp-content/uploads/Crypto-20.jpg
https://i.redd.it/ugwnwdn7vvh01.jpg
https://images1.calcalist.co.il/PicServer3/2017/12/12/778671/backboneserver_l.jpg

That last pic is from the following article:

https://www.calcalistech.com/ctech/articles/0,7340,L-3733744,00.html

One cannot artificially cap demand; criticising AIBs and retailers responding to all these pressures is just dumb (you are aware that these companies have all sorts of increased costs, yes? They have to pay more for the restricted supply options, and these custom web site changes don't appear out of thin air). Atm the only things that can really help are an end to the stupid  lockdowns & restrictions and the reopening of normal supply chains. Some believe that a crypto crash would be a solution, but that his its own serious consequences in other ways (because govts and conventional investors are now spending big on crypto aswell).

text:
to be fair to amd, they kinda had to put 16gb on the rx6800 series, they had a 256bit bus, so it was either 8 or 16 and 8 probably would be enough, so 16. the 6700xt has the same issue but with a less wide bus, so 6 or 12, so they choose 12, which is completely reasonable considering their 6800 has 16gb and the 6700xt should have like about 70% the CUs

Nvidia has a similar limitation, but they were clearly planning on selling the rtx 3060 with 6gb of vram and had to scramble because of the rx 6700 xt, so released the 12gb card.

i don't really blame anyone too much for it, but clearly for AMD, they planned their product stack properly from the start, while nvidia nerfed the rtx 3080 with only 10gb of vram to encourage people to buy the rtx 3090

Jay, you are straight-up wrong about the Newegg Shuffle. It's the ONLY fair system out there that also happens to be incredibly effective at selling hardware to someone other than scalpers for once.

text:
Jay has been putting out a lot of videos with false information lately.  Leaks have been verified many times over that the 6700xt will release with 12gb of vram, not 16.  Also, each die is made together (GA102, GA106, etc) and yields are only split between dies, so a bad binned GA102 will not be used as a GA106.  Nvidia may still use a bad binned GA102 for a GPU that would use a GA106 (the 2060ko was a TU104 die cut down to a 2060 core count, which is why it performed much better than other 2060 cards in blender)

I also find his view on Newegg shuffle to be a privileged view.  It's his opinion, so I don't argue with him stating it.  But it's a privilege to be able to be able to wait for a release the moment it happens, and the newegg shuffle helps to remove some of this privilege by expanding the window of opportunity to buy to a few hours instead of a few....seconds?

I do absolutely agree that the larger VRAM sizes are out there more as marketing, though certain workloads may need the VRAM more than the compute power and the 3060 is a great opportunity for those people.

text:
Jay,
Have you seen the details of the "Supply Chain" discussions in D.C. this week?  They've decided to focus on 4 categories:
1:  Medical, includes Covid.  2: Defense.  3: Battery Tech, primarily for Electric Vehicles and 4: Semiconductors of all types.

Earlier this month all of the big players in the semiconductor industry including Intel, AMD, Qualcomm,  and even Samsung and other Asian manufacturers co-signed a letter to Biden suggesting they all want to build Fab plants in the US so they have a reliable alternate source of materials.  They were trying the waters to see what kind of funds might be available to help expand existing or build new plants.

Considering the push for higher quality job creation and training, plus rebuilding the economy after the pandemic, There's a good chance that within the next couple of years we may see parts from these new plants.
